title: Telling it your way
job: Retell a known story in your own register
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: YENNAL YENNAL-E OPENS A TALE. Once upon a time, doubled. L4-M8 already bought both tokens for yennal-e-neun, in the old days, and the doubling is what turns a memory into a story.

A KOREAN RETELLING STAYS IN THE PAST. English reaches for the historic present to make a story live — so he walks in. Korean has no narrative present at all, and a tale told in the present reads as a plot summary.
REGISTER IS THE ONLY VARIABLE. The same events go to a friend in -yo and to a room in L4-M7's -(seu)pnida. What moves is the ending and how much the narrator comments; the events never move.
THE QUOTED LINE KEEPS ITS OWN ENDING. L3-M5's rago takes whatever the character actually said, ending and all, and haesseoyo closes it. Nothing inside the quotation marks is adjusted.
ALGO BONI IS THE TURN. L4-M10's as it turned out, reused whole and never re-taught. A retold tale wants exactly one of them.
GYEOLGUK AND KKEUT CLOSE DIFFERENT THINGS. gyeolguk is in the end and sits on the last event; kkeut-ieyo is what you say when the telling itself is over.
THE FRAME NARRATOR MAKES IT A RETELLING. geu iyagi-neun ... iyagi-yeyo — that story is a story about — is the sentence that separates telling a tale from reciting one.
NO STORYBOOK -(NEU)NDA AND NO BANMAL. A tale told to a child lives in both and this course teaches neither, so the tale opens with yennal yennal-e and continues in -yo or in -(seu)pnida.

sentences.cue: Once upon a time, an old woman lived in the countryside.

words.note: Learn it as one opening. L4-M8's yennal is the old days; doubled and marked with -e it stops being a memory and becomes a tale.
The past of L4-M2's sarayo, and the verb every Korean tale opens on. There lived is the whole first sentence.

sentences.trap: English once upon a time can be dropped and the story still starts. yennal yennal-e cannot: without it the first sentence is a claim about somebody's grandmother.

variations.cue: An old woman lived in the countryside.
variations.changed: the opening dropped: a fact, and no longer a tale

variations.cue: Once upon a time, an old woman lived in the countryside.
variations.changed: the deferential ending: the same tale told to a room

mistake.why: The opening puts the tale in the past and the verb has to follow it. Korean has no historic present, so a present-tense verb here simply contradicts the first two words.

sentences.usage: Starting a tale everybody in the room already knows.
sentences.mnemonic: Say the old day twice and the story begins.

sentences.display: Halmeoni-neun san-e gasseoyo. Geurigo horangi-reul mannasseoyo.
sentences.script: 할머니는 산에 갔어요. 그리고 호랑이를 만났어요.
sentences.cue: The old woman went to the mountain. And she met a tiger.
sentences.literal: grandmother-TOP mountain-to went. and tiger-OBJ met

words.note: The one animal a Korean tale can hardly do without. It costs a key; a tale with three named characters would cost three.

sentences.trap: English keeps the subject alive with pronouns — she went, then she met. Korean marks the old woman once with -neun and then says nothing more about who is acting.
sentences.sound: HAL-meo-ni-neun SA-ne GA-sseo-yo. GEU-ri-go HO-rang-i-reul MAN-na-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: The old woman went to the mountain.
variations.changed: the first event alone

variations.cue: The old woman met a tiger.
variations.changed: the journey dropped: straight to the meeting

mistake.display: Halmeoni-neun san-e gasseoyo. Geurigo halmeoni-neun horangi-reul mannasseoyo.
mistake.script: 할머니는 산에 갔어요. 그리고 할머니는 호랑이를 만났어요.
mistake.why: Naming the same person again in the next sentence sounds like a second old woman. Once the topic is set with -neun it stays set until something changes it.

sentences.usage: Moving a tale on one event at a time.
sentences.mnemonic: One topic, then a chain of events under it.

sentences.display: Horangi-ga "Bap-eul juseyo" rago haesseoyo. Halmeoni-neun museoweosseoyo.
sentences.cue: The tiger said, give me some rice. The old woman was afraid.
sentences.literal: tiger-SUBJ rice-OBJ give-QUOT said. grandmother-TOP was-afraid

words.note: The past of L3-M6's museoweoyo. It covers both was afraid and was frightening, so the same word can be said of the woman and of the tiger.

sentences.trap: English rewrites a quotation to fit the sentence — she asked him to give her rice. Korean leaves the line exactly as it was spoken, honorific ending and all, and only rago and haesseoyo are added around it.
sentences.sound: HO-rang-i-ga BA-beul JU-se-yo ra-go HAE-sseo-yo. HAL-meo-ni-neun MU-seo-weo-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: The tiger said, give me some rice.
variations.changed: the quotation alone, with no reaction

variations.cue: The old woman was afraid.
variations.changed: the reaction alone, with the line withheld

mistake.why: Bending the quoted line towards the reporting sentence is an English habit. The whole point of -rago is that it takes the words as they came.

sentences.usage: Putting a line of speech into a tale you are retelling.
sentences.mnemonic: Quote it as said, then rago haesseoyo.

sentences.display: Geuraeseo halmeoni-neun domangchyeosseoyo. Algo boni horangi-do museoweosseoyo.
sentences.script: 그래서 할머니는 도망쳤어요. 알고 보니 호랑이도 무서웠어요.
sentences.cue: So the old woman ran away. As it turned out, the tiger was frightened too.
sentences.literal: so grandmother-TOP fled. knowing seeing tiger-also was-afraid

words.note: One event verb, in the past like everything else in a tale. Said do-mang-chyeo-sseo-yo, four beats before the ending.

sentences.trap: English marks the twist with tone of voice or with it turned out that. Korean marks it with L4-M10's algo boni, in the slot before the clause, and a tale wants only one of them.
sentences.sound: GEU-rae-seo HAL-meo-ni-neun DO-mang-chyeo-sseo-yo. AL-go BO-ni HO-rang-i-do MU-seo-weo-sseo-yo.

variations.cue: The old woman ran away.
variations.changed: the join and the twist dropped

variations.cue: As it turned out, the tiger was frightened too.
variations.changed: the twist alone: the line that makes the tale worth retelling

mistake.display: Algo boni halmeoni-neun domangchyeosseoyo. Geuraeseo horangi-do museoweosseoyo.
mistake.script: 알고 보니 할머니는 도망쳤어요. 그래서 호랑이도 무서웠어요.
mistake.why: The twist has been put on the ordinary event and the ordinary join on the twist. algo boni belongs on the thing nobody expected, which here is the tiger.

sentences.usage: Landing the turn a listener is waiting for.
sentences.mnemonic: algo boni: only once you look do you know.

sentences.cue: In the end the old woman came home.

words.note: Marks the last event of the story, not the end of the telling. It sits at the front of its clause, like L5-M6's discourse words.

sentences.trap: English finally can mean at last, thank goodness. gyeolguk is flatter than that: it reports where the events came to rest, with no relief in it.

variations.cue: In the end the old woman went home.
variations.changed: gasseoyo for wasseoyo: told from away rather than from here

variations.cue: The old woman came home.
variations.changed: the closing word dropped: one more event, not the last

mistake.why: gyeolguk announces that this is the last event, and an announcement that arrives after the event has nothing left to announce. It goes at the front.

sentences.usage: Bringing the events of a tale to rest.
sentences.mnemonic: gyeolguk is where it all ended up.

sentences.cue: And that is the end of the story.

words.note: A noun, so it takes L1-M1's copula. gyeolguk closed the events; kkeut-ieyo closes the telling and hands the floor back.

sentences.trap: English the end is a caption on a page. kkeut-ieyo is spoken out loud at the close of a told story, and leaving it out is what makes a retelling trail off.

variations.cue: The story is over.
variations.changed: the join dropped: a flatter close

variations.cue: And that is the end.
variations.changed: the subject dropped, as it usually is

mistake.why: gyeolguk is an adverb sitting in front of a clause, not a noun a copula can take. The word that ends a telling is kkeut.

sentences.usage: Handing the floor back when you have finished.
sentences.mnemonic: kkeut, and the room can speak again.

sentences.cue: That folk tale is a good one.

words.note: The kind of story, where L5-M2's iyagi is any story at all. A dongwha is the shared one, which is why it costs the teller no plot at all.

sentences.trap: English folk tale sounds academic. dongwha is the ordinary word a Korean adult uses for the stories everybody was told, so it belongs in the conversation and not in a footnote.

variations.cue: That folk tale was a good one.
variations.changed: the past: a verdict on the telling just finished

variations.cue: Folk tales are good.
variations.changed: the demonstrative dropped: the whole genre

mistake.why: L5-M2 taught jaemi as the noun fun. Saying the tale IS fun rather than that it HAS interest is not a Korean sentence; the adjective jaemiisseoyo does this job.

sentences.usage: Commenting on the tale, once you have told it.
sentences.mnemonic: dongwha is the story children get; iyagi is any story at all.

sentences.cue: The main character of that folk tale was afraid.

words.note: The word that lets you talk about a tale rather than inside it. With L5-M4's -ui it belongs to the story that holds it.

sentences.trap: English can say the main character was scared and mean the reader was. Korean cannot: jueingong is strictly the person inside the tale, and a comment about the listener needs its own sentence.

variations.cue: The main character of that folk tale ran away.
variations.changed: a different event reported about the same character

variations.cue: The main character was afraid.
variations.changed: the tale dropped: everybody knows which one

mistake.why: Two nouns pushed together leave it open which belongs to which. -ui is what ties the character to the tale, and in a sentence about a story that link is the point.

sentences.usage: Talking about a tale from outside it.
sentences.mnemonic: jueingong is the one the tale is about.

sentences.cue: That story is a story about a tiger.

words.note: L5-M2's iyagi with L1-M1's copula. In the frame sentence the same noun stands at both ends, and the middle says what the story is about.

sentences.trap: English says a story about a tiger and the about does the work. Korean puts the topic bare in front of iyagi, with no particle at all, so the two nouns simply lean together.

variations.cue: That story is a story about an old woman.
variations.changed: a different subject in the middle slot

variations.cue: It is a story about a tiger.
variations.changed: the frame opened dropped: the summary alone

mistake.why: -ui would make it the tiger's own story, told by or belonging to him. A story about a subject leaves the two nouns bare and next to each other.

sentences.usage: Announcing what a retelling is going to be about.
sentences.mnemonic: Story-topic-story: the frame closes on the word it opened with.

sentences.cue: Once upon a time, an old woman lived in the countryside.

words.note: The same event as S01's sarasseoyo in L4-M7's deferential ending. Nothing else in the sentence changes, which is the whole lesson of this module.

sentences.trap: English shifts a retelling by changing words — the bedtime version and the lecture version share almost no vocabulary. Korean shifts it by changing the ending and leaving the words alone.

variations.cue: Once upon a time, an old woman lived in the countryside.
variations.changed: back to -yo: the same tale, told to one friend

variations.cue: An old woman lived in the countryside.
variations.changed: the opening dropped: a report, not a tale

mistake.display: Yennal yennal-e halmeoni-ga sigol-e sarasseumnida. Geurigo horangi-reul mannasseoyo.
mistake.script: 옛날 옛날에 할머니가 시골에 살았습니다. 그리고 호랑이를 만났어요.
mistake.why: The register slipped back after one sentence. A retelling holds one level all the way through, and L5-M10 is where a switch inside a piece is allowed — and only with a reason on the page.

sentences.usage: Telling the same tale across a counter or to a room.
sentences.mnemonic: Same tale, new ending, nothing else touched.

comprehensionPool.cue: Once upon a time, an old woman lived in the countryside.
The old woman met a tiger.
The tiger said, give me some rice.
So the old woman ran away.
As it turned out, the tiger was frightened too.
In the end the old woman came home.
And that is the end of the story.
That folk tale is a good one.
The main character of that folk tale was afraid.
That story is a story about a tiger.
Once upon a time, an old woman lived in the countryside.
